\chapter{When the Calendar Stopped Naming}
\label{ch:monate-zahlen}
\hlchaptermodality{14}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the last six German months and say which of them are numbers rather than names.}

Two months named for men who could order it -- Julius Caesar, who rebuilt the calendar, and Augustus, who took the next one -- and then the naming stops. September through Dezember are septem, octo, novem and decem, counted from Maerz where the Roman year began. German's own seven, eight, nine and ten sound like none of them, and never had to.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[der Juli]{der Juli — \textquotedblleft{}July\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-juli}



\begin{quote}
Six months named for gods, festivals and guesses. From here the calendar changes what it is doing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Juli}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Juli} — \textquotedblleft{}July.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Latin \emph{Julius}, and not a god: \textbf{Julius Caesar}. He rebuilt the Roman calendar into something that tracked the sun, and the month of his birth was renamed for him while he was alive to see it.

\emph{Juni} and \emph{Juli} differ by one letter and one sound. Take them slowly as a pair: \emph{YOO-nee}, \emph{YOO-lee}.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{j-as-y} — English \emph{y} again, as in \emph{Januar} and \emph{Juni}.
  \item \texttt{ie-long-ee} — and a long \emph{ee} at the end.
\end{itemize}

Because the two are so close, German speakers arranging a date will often say \emph{Julei} for July, stretching it away from \emph{Juni}. You will hear it; you do not have to say it.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Juli\textquotedblright{} — YOO-lee
  \item the pair, slowly — \textquotedblleft{}Juni, Juli\textquotedblright{}
  \item who it is — \textquotedblleft{}Julius Caesar, not a god\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Juni, Juli.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}July.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Juli}.) And \textquotedblleft{}June\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Der Juni}.) Which one is a god? (\emph{\textbf{Juni}} — \textbf{Juno}.) Which one is a man? (\emph{\textbf{Juli}} — \textbf{Caesar}.) Next: the man who took the hint.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der August]{der August — \textquotedblleft{}August\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-august}



\begin{quote}
Caesar took a month. His heir noticed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der August}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der August} — \textquotedblleft{}August.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The emperor \textbf{Augustus}, Caesar's adopted son, who had the next month renamed for himself. Two men in a row, side by side in the year, and then it stops: \textbf{no month after this one is named for anybody at all.}

The weight falls on the second syllable in German — \emph{au-GUST} — where English puts it on the first.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{au-diphthong} — \emph{au} is one gliding vowel, the \emph{ow} of English \emph{how}.
  \item \texttt{st-initial-scht} — the \emph{st} here is \textbf{inside} the word, not at the start, so it stays a plain \emph{st}. German's \emph{sht} happens at the beginning of a word, and this is the contrast that shows you where the boundary is.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der August\textquotedblright{} — au-GUST
  \item the two men, in order — \textquotedblleft{}Juli, August\textquotedblright{}
  \item what happens next — \textquotedblleft{}the naming stops\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Juli, August.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}August.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der August}.) Which syllable is stressed? (\textbf{The second} — au-GUST.) Who is it? (\textbf{The emperor Augustus}.) How many months are named for men? (\textbf{Two} — and they are next to each other.) Next: what the calendar does once it runs out of names.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der September]{der September — \textquotedblleft{}September\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-september}



\begin{quote}
You have the Latin number for seven from a chapter about counting. Here it is again, wearing a month.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der September}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der September} — \textquotedblleft{}September.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Latin \emph{september}, from \emph{\textbf{septem}} — \textbf{seven}. Count from \emph{März}, where the Roman year started, and September lands seventh.

The year was later moved to start in January. The name was not moved with it, so a word meaning \textquotedblleft{}seventh\textquotedblright{} now sits in the ninth slot, in German exactly as in English, and has done for two thousand years.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-e-german} — three clear short \emph{e}s: \emph{sep-TEM-ber}.
  \item \texttt{r-final} — closing on the soft \emph{r}.
\end{itemize}

The stress is on the middle syllable, as in English.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der September\textquotedblright{} — sep-TEM-ber
  \item the Latin number inside it — \textquotedblleft{}septem, seven\textquotedblright{}
  \item the German seven beside it — \textquotedblleft{}sieben\textquotedblright{}
  \item where the count starts — \textquotedblleft{}März\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}September — septem — sieben.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}September.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der September}.) What number is inside it? (\emph{\textbf{Septem}} — \textbf{seven}.) Which position does it actually hold now? (\textbf{Ninth}.) Why the mismatch? (\textbf{The year used to start in März}.) What is German's own seven? (\emph{\textbf{Sieben}}.) Next: eight.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Oktober]{der Oktober — \textquotedblleft{}October\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-oktober}



\begin{quote}
The same trick as September, one number along.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Oktober}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Oktober} — \textquotedblleft{}October.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Latin \emph{october}, from \emph{\textbf{octo}} — \textbf{eight}. Eighth from \emph{März}, tenth on the calendar you use.

Notice the spelling. English writes \emph{Oc-}, keeping the Latin \emph{c}. German writes \emph{Ok-}, because German spells that sound with a \textbf{k} and applies its own rule to a borrowed word. Same word, same origin, one letter of local habit.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-o-german} — a clean rounded \emph{o}, held steady rather than gliding as English \emph{oh} does.
  \item \texttt{r-final} — and the soft closing \emph{r}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{ok-TOH-ber}, weight in the middle.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Oktober\textquotedblright{} — ok-TOH-ber
  \item the Latin number — \textquotedblleft{}octo, eight\textquotedblright{}
  \item the German eight — \textquotedblleft{}acht\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair so far — \textquotedblleft{}September, Oktober\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Oktober — octo — acht.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}October.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Oktober}.) Which letter does German use where English keeps a \emph{c}? (\textbf{A} \emph{k}.) What number is inside? (\emph{\textbf{Octo}} — \textbf{eight}.) German's own eight? (\emph{\textbf{Acht}}.) Next: nine.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der November]{der November — \textquotedblleft{}November\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-november}



\begin{quote}
Spelled exactly as in English. Said differently, on one letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der November}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der November} — \textquotedblleft{}November.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Latin \emph{november}, from \emph{\textbf{novem}} — \textbf{nine}. Ninth from \emph{März}, eleventh now.

German and English write this month with the same eleven letters. That is rarer than it looks, and it happens here because both took the word from Latin without touching it.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{v-as-f} — German \emph{v} is an \textbf{f}. The month is \emph{no-FEM-ber}.
  \item \texttt{r-final} — soft closing \emph{r}, as on the two before it.
\end{itemize}

This is the one letter where the identical spelling stops being identical. A German reading \emph{November} aloud produces something an English ear does not expect, and nothing about the page warns you.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der November\textquotedblright{} — no-FEM-ber
  \item the Latin number — \textquotedblleft{}novem, nine\textquotedblright{}
  \item the German nine — \textquotedblleft{}neun\textquotedblright{}
  \item three in order — \textquotedblleft{}September, Oktober, November\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}November — no-FEM-ber.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}November.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der November} — no-FEM-ber.) How is German \emph{v} said? (\textbf{As an} \emph{f}.) What number is inside? (\emph{\textbf{Novem}} — \textbf{nine}.) German's own nine? (\emph{\textbf{Neun}}.) Next: ten, and the end of the year.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Dezember]{der Dezember — \textquotedblleft{}December\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-dezember}



\begin{quote}
The last month, and a letter whose sound you were given with a number.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Dezember}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Dezember} — \textquotedblleft{}December.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Latin \emph{december}, from \emph{\textbf{decem}} — \textbf{ten}. Tenth from \emph{März}, twelfth now, and the last of the four months that are nothing but numbers.

Where English writes \emph{De-c-}, German writes \emph{De-z-}.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — German \emph{z} is \textbf{ts}, the sound you were given on \emph{zehn}. So the month opens \emph{de-TSEM-}, not \emph{de-SEM-}.
  \item \texttt{r-final} — and it closes on the same soft \emph{r} as the other three.
\end{itemize}

That is the whole difference between the German and English versions of one Latin word: \emph{c} became \emph{z}, because German already had a letter for that sound.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Dezember\textquotedblright{} — de-TSEM-ber
  \item the German ten, same opening sound — \textquotedblleft{}zehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item the Latin number — \textquotedblleft{}decem, ten\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four in order — \textquotedblleft{}September, Oktober, November, Dezember\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Dezember — de-TSEM-ber.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}December.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Dezember}.) How does German \emph{z} sound? (\textbf{Ts}.) Which number gave you that? (\emph{\textbf{Zehn}}.) What number is inside the month? (\emph{\textbf{Decem}} — \textbf{ten}.) Next: the four of them together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — the second half of the year}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-zahlmonate}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Six names, of which four are not really names.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the four that count in Latin}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the month} & \textbf{the Latin inside} & \textbf{German's own word} \\
\midrule
\emph{September} & \emph{septem} & \emph{sieben} \\
\emph{Oktober} & \emph{octo} & \emph{acht} \\
\emph{November} & \emph{novem} & \emph{neun} \\
\emph{Dezember} & \emph{decem} & \emph{zehn} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read across each row and hear that nothing rhymes. German counts in one language and dates in another, and never reconciled the two — because there was never any occasion to.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
The second half of the year is a record of a calendar running out of ideas.

\emph{ \emph{\textbf{Juli}} — \textbf{Julius Caesar}, who rebuilt the calendar and took a month. } \emph{\textbf{August}} — \textbf{Augustus}, who took the next one. \emph{ \emph{\textbf{September}} to \emph{\textbf{Dezember}} — nobody at all. Seven, eight, nine, ten, counted from }März\emph{, where the year used to begin.}

Two men who could order a month renamed did so, one after the other, and then the practice stopped. What was left was arithmetic, and the arithmetic stopped being true the moment the year moved to January — which nobody thought worth fixing, and so it stands.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all six — \textquotedblleft{}Juli, August, September, Oktober, November, Dezember\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two men — \textquotedblleft{}Caesar, Augustus\textquotedblright{}
  \item each Latin number with its German twin — \textquotedblleft{}septem, sieben; octo, acht; novem, neun; decem, zehn\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one that begins with a ts — \textquotedblleft{}Dezember\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one whose v is an f — \textquotedblleft{}November\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}September, Oktober, November, Dezember.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the last four months. (\textbf{September, Oktober, November, Dezember}.) What are they named for? (\textbf{Numbers — seven, eight, nine, ten}.) Counted from where? (\emph{\textbf{März}}.) Which two are named for men? (\emph{\textbf{Juli}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{August}}.) Do German's own numbers sound like the Latin ones inside the months? (\textbf{No} — and they never had to.)
\end{tcolorbox}
